newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ericsson launches smallest GSM phone.
newsitem.headline: Ericsson launches smallest GSM phone.

text.p: Swedish telecommunications group LM Ericsson AB unveiled the smallest GSM portable phone on Tuesday and said it expected continued price pressure in the world market for handsets.

On the eve of the GSM World Congress in the Mediterranean resort of Cannes, the equipment maker also unveiled a concept for wireless office and business applications to allow mobile workers to use a company's telecommunications infrastructure fully, including an Intranet computer network.
"In GSM, we expect price erosion of some 20 to 25 percent in 1997," Jan Ahrenbring, marketing director for Ericsson Business Area Mobile Phones and Terminals, told Reuters.
"Everybody is ramping up volume and there are big economies of scale. But we still cannot meet demand," he added.

Ericsson last week reported a 33 percent increase in 1996 pre-tax profits to 10.15 billion crowns ($1.4 billion) on a 26 percent rise in sales to 124.27 billion crowns. It said at the time it did not see an end to the price pressure.
To fight the price erosion, Ericsson is launching new products and extending the range of its products.
"In three years' time we can provide a phone the size of a watch. But do consumers want that?" Ahrenbring asked.
Ericsson's newest product, the GF 788, is as big as a pack of cigarettes. It is 105 by 49 by 24 millimetres, weighs 135 grams and delivers three hours of talk time with 60 hours standby.

Helene Barnekow, global product manager for the GF 788, said the telephone should not only be functional but "should also be nice, sophisticated and beautiful". The set is available in four colours because it is seen as a "personal accessory".
Ericsson will start deliveries of the GF 788 in March and it will be available in all GSM (Global System for Mobiles) markets in the second quarter.
It has an easy to use menu, which can be personalised, and will also allow data transfer.

The price of the new phone is difficult to define because Ericsson is not the end-seller but delivers to GSM operators. However, Ericsson officials said they believed the new phone to be 30 to 40 percent more expensive than their GF 388, which in France would lead to a price of 3,500 to 4,000 francs ($609 to $700).
Ericsson expects the number of world digital subscribers to rise to 500 million by 2001 from 50 million in 1996.
The Swedish company also delivers the infrastructure to GSM operators. There are now 149 operators in more than 100 countries providing digital mobile telecoms with the GSM standard.

Marketing vice-president Eric Berthels unveiled the company's "Wireless Office and Business Applications Concept". This allows operators to deliver wireless voice and data applications that include a virtual private network, allowing workers to use their phone anywhere as if they were inside the company.
Users will have one personal number for voice, data and fax messages, can screen incoming calls, choose to ignore some callers at times and allow specific callers to reach them at any time.
Ericsson expects the infrastructure needs for such mobile business applications to exceed $5 billion in 2002. ($ = 7.456 Swedish Crowns) ($ = 5.748 French Francs)
